sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (fill in the blanks, true/false, one word or phrase, match).

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) All members are related to each other by blood in a tribe. (b) All members of a tribe are not equal.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – all members are equal in status.

questions.q: The caste system was so entrenched in the psyche of people of India. Examine with two examples.
questions.answer: Even plants were divided on the basis of varna and one text prescribed varying sizes of houses according to the varnas; sects of reformers like Basava and Kabir, and Sikhs, Muslims and Christians, developed caste features.

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) The Dharmashastras and Smritis tried to fix the duties of each caste. (b) Relations between castes were not generally governed by endogamy, commensality and craft exclusiveness.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – they were governed by these rules.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: In ancient India the four ______ of life began not with the physical birth, but with the ______ ceremony.
Answer in a phrase: (a) What is meant by hypergamous marriage? (b) What is pratiloma marriage?
questions.answer: (a) A man of a high caste marries a woman of a lower caste (anuloma). (b) A man of a low caste marries a woman of a high caste (hypogamous).

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) A clan is an exogamous institution whereas a tribe is endogamous. (b) Tribes have a strong sense of private property.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – it is least visible.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The four aims of life are dharma, artha, ______ and ______.
Answer in a phrase: (a) Name the fourth ashrama. (b) What is shraddha?
questions.answer: (a) Sanyasa. (b) The rite of commemorating the ancestors that binds family members.

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) Joint families may be matrilineal in Kerala. (b) Hindu Acts of 1955–56 govern Muslims.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – they govern Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs and Jains.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: Manu noted ______ castes. The Kayasthas were traditionally ______.
Answer in a phrase: (a) Name two Vedic tribes. (b) Name two tribes of the Central zone.
questions.answer: (a) Bharatas and Yadus (Purus, Anus). (b) Santhals and Ho (Baiga, Munda).

questions.q: Mark true or false: (a) Todas practise buffalo herding. (b) Gujjars are a polyandrous tribe.
questions.answer: (a) True. (b) False – the Khasas are polyandrous; Gujjars are pastoral.

questions.q: Answer in a phrase: (a) What did the Arthashastra say about slavery? (b) Who became commander-in-chief of Alauddin Khilji among slaves?
questions.answer: (a) A man could be a slave by birth, voluntary sale, capture in war or judicial punishment. (b) Malik Kafur.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: The sacred thread ceremony is the ______ samskara. The Jajmani system is breaking up due to ______ and urbanisation.
Mark true or false: (a) Untouchability is not a punishable crime. (b) Gandhi launched a campaign against it.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in about 25 words.

questions.q: Discuss the changes which came in Indian society during the Maurya and post-Mauryan period.
questions.answer: Urban centres, trade and crafts grew; guilds (shreni) became important and later castes; new groups (Shakas, Kushanas, Parthians, Indo-Greeks) arrived; Buddhism and Jainism challenged Brahmanism; the caste system started to crystallise and untouchability became a separate category.

or.q: Why did guilds become important during the Mauryan and post-Mauryan period?
or.answer: They controlled craft production and trade, acted as bankers and trustees, provided technical education and had their own court and law (shreni-dharma).

questions.q: Explain the beginning of untouchability in Indian society during ancient times.
questions.answer: The notion of purity and pollution led to the antyajas (outside Brahmanical society) taking root in the late Vedic period; it became a separate category in the Buddha's age, and groups like chandalas, hunters, fishermen, leather workers and sweepers became untouchables.

or.q: Explain the efforts made to abolish untouchability in the modern period.
or.answer: Gandhi campaigned and called them Harijans; Ambedkar opened schools; the Constitution declared untouchability a punishable offence; education and social movements bridged the gap.

questions.q: Examine any two specific features of the life of tribal people.
questions.answer: They live in relative isolation in hills and forests with roots in the soil; their language, institutions, beliefs and customs differ from others; members are equal and share resources with little private property.

or.q: How does a tribe become numerically important? Name one such tribe.
or.answer: When its population is large – the Gonds, Bhils and Santhals each have more than 30 lakh.

questions.q: What is the meaning of 'dvijas'?
questions.answer: Twice-born – members of the three upper varnas (Brahmana, Kshatriya and Vaishya) who were entitled to the sacred thread ceremony.

questions.q: Write the problems of the tribal people of the Eastern zone.
questions.answer: Economic backwardness, exploitation by forest officials and contractors, land alienation, disease and displacement due to industrial projects.

questions.q: What is the Jajmani system?
questions.answer: A complementary relationship in rural society between dominant peasant castes and service and artisan castes who received fixed shares of produce or land for their services; it is breaking up due to monetisation and urbanisation.

questions.q: Name the four ashramas.
What is the tribal sub-plan?
questions.answer: A comprehensive strategy begun in the Fifth Five-Year Plan to end exploitation of tribals, promote their socio-economic development, bridge the development gap and improve quality of life.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 40–50 words.

questions.q: Discuss any three major problems of tribal people living in the North Zone of India.
questions.answer: Inaccessibility of their hilly areas, lack of communication and roads, poverty and illiteracy, and land alienation; the tribes include Khasa, Tharu, Bhoksa, Bhotias, Gujjars and Jaunsaris.

or.q: Discuss any three major problems of tribal people living in the North-East Zone of India.
or.answer: Ecological degradation from shifting cultivation, inaccessibility and lack of communication, and isolation that created hostility to the mainstream.

questions.q: Explain three types of marriages based on the number of spouses.
questions.answer: Monogamy (one spouse at a time, the most common), polygamy (more than one wife, practised by kings and the rich, now illegal except for Muslims with conditions) and polyandry (more than one husband, as in the Khasas and in Draupadi's case, valid in some hill communities).

or.q: Explain the preconditions for arranged marriages among Hindus of India.
or.answer: Parents arrange marriage within the same caste but of different gotras and outside the prohibited degrees (pravaras – seven generations paternal and five maternal).

questions.q: Explain the four purusharthas and ashramas.
questions.answer: The aims of life are dharma, artha, kama and moksha. For these a life is divided into brahmacharya (education), grihastha (family life and livelihood), vanaprastha (retirement and detachment) and sanyasa (renunciation).

questions.q: Describe the institution of slavery in India.
questions.answer: Slavery differed from the Greek and Roman: a slave could be by birth, voluntary sale, capture or punishment; slaves were domestic servants and members of the household; masters had no rights over their lives; slave markets existed in Vijayanagara and the Portuguese traded slaves at Goa; Cornwallis attacked it and the trade is now prohibited.

questions.q: Describe the position of women in the Vedic and post-Vedic periods.
questions.answer: In the Vedic period women took part in tribal affairs, composed hymns and chose husbands at a mature age; later law books reduced them to Shudra status, gave only stridhana, closed Vedic knowledge to them, and early marriage, sati and the veil became common.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 150–200 words.

questions.q: Describe any five special features of tribals.
questions.answer: Tribals are among the oldest inhabitants (adivasis) with roots in the soil; they live in relative isolation in hills and forests; all members are related by blood, equal in status and descended from a common ancestor; they have equal access to resources and little private property; social differences exist only by age and sex; a tribe is endogamous and made of exogamous clans; they have a distinct language, institutions, beliefs and customs; development and protection need priority and 427 communities are Scheduled Tribes.

or.answer: Early Vedic tribes were the Bharatas, Yadus, Turvasas, Druhyus, Purus and Anus with a Raja who was first among equals; the main distinction was between Vedic tribes and the dasa varna with alien language, dark complexion and different gods; this differentiation grew into the varna system.

questions.q: Examine the evolution of the caste system in India.
questions.answer: From the tribal society with varna (colour) differences, wars, loot and unequal wealth produced the four varnas. Buddhism and Jainism ridiculed it but did not remove it. Guilds of craftsmen and traders became castes; new groups arrived; between 500 BC and 500 AD the system crystallised and castes multiplied with crafts, anuloma and pratiloma marriages and inclusion of tribes. After the 5th century Vaishyas and Shudras merged as peasants; in the south Shudras were pure and impure; Rajputs, Kayasthas and Marathas became castes; later surnames were added; reformers' sects and even Sikhs, Muslims and Christians developed caste features.

questions.q: Critically examine the position of women in the history of Indian society.
questions.answer: It is the story of progressive decline. In the Vedic period women took part in tribal affairs and composed hymns; later law books gave them Shudra status and only stridhana, denied Vedic study, promoted early marriage, sati and the veil. Reformers and modern education led to the ban on sati (1829), widow remarriage (1856), the Hindu Marriage Act (1955) and daughters' property rights, improving their condition.

questions.q: Discuss the family and marriage institutions in India.
questions.answer: The traditional family is the joint family under a patriarch, bound by shraddha and governed by Mitakshara or Dayabhaga; nuclear families are growing and matrilineal ones exist in Kerala and the North-East. Marriage is a samskara; there are anuloma and pratiloma alliances, and monogamy, polygamy and polyandry; arranged marriages are within the caste and outside the same gotra and pravara; divorce was once not allowed but is now legal on grounds like cruelty and desertion; personal laws differ by religion.

questions.q: Explain the tribal zones of India and the problems faced by tribals.
questions.answer: India has seven zones: North (Khasa, Gujjars – inaccessibility, poverty), North-East (Nagas, Khasi – shifting cultivation, isolation), Central (Santhals, Ho, Baiga – land alienation, indebtedness), Southern (Todas, Chenchus – backwardness, language loss), Eastern (Paraja, Kondhas – exploitation, displacement), Western (Bhils, Meenas) and Islands (Jarwas, Onges – threat of extinction). The government has a tribal sub-plan since the Fifth Plan.
